speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

Mr. Speaker, on a government motion to resolve the house into committee of supply it is not only a traditional opportunity but it is, as I conceive it, the duty of the official opposition to raise questions that are matters of essential grievances on the part of parliament and the Canadian people.
Here we have before the house a matter of serious parliamentary concern. It should not have been necessary, indeed, to introduce an amendment to debate the matter in the house, but it has become necessary because of the fact that this government is so wedded to power, arbitrary power. Not only is the government reluctant to give up power, but, sir, it is reluctant even to submit such questions for discussion in the house.
It will not be forgotten that as early as November 18 of the present session, noting that the speech from the throne was silent on the important subject of the Emergency Powers Act, I made so bold as to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this question, as reported at page 122 of Hansard:
May I ask the Prime Minister if it is the intention of the government to ask parliament at this present session to extend the Emergency Powers Act?
To that question the Prime Minister made this not very informative reply:
That is a matter of policy about which information will be communicated to the house in due time.
What is "due time"? Apparently "due time" has not yet arrived. Therefore those of us who are not prepared to bide the time of a tardy government consider this an eminently proper occasion to put this matter squarely before the house. And the house will have an inescapable opportunity to say whether it is proper to condone, under today's circumstances, the continuance of arbitrary powers in this government.
The government is having trouble to make up its mind on this question, as the Prime Minister conveyed to the house yesterday.

Well, let us take due account of the indecision of the government, and let the house, then, assist this indecisive government with respect to this question.
What is the background? The background is one of a succession of statutes under which this government has been seeking sweeping powers ever since the emergent days of the war. First it was the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act; then it was the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act; then it was the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act, followed by the Emergency Powers Act-and now by the various extensions of the Emergency Powers Act.
Sir, our amendment will invite the house to record its opinion on this question. The amendment is as follows:
this house desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
Sir, the Emergency Powers Act is a notorious measure; it is time it was expunged' from the statute books of Canada. It is a blot on the records of the Canadian parliament. That statute is the measure of the extent to which, under today's conditions, there has been under the pressure and leadership of the present government a departure from parliamentary processes and responsible government. This statute, if it is left where it is, will continue in force until May 31. Sir, it should not be allowed to run its course; it should be removed from the statute books of Canada without further delay.
Oh, oh.

There will be an opportunity for my hon. friend, who took a very praiseworthy course on an earlier occasion, again to express that true conception of the relationship between the government and parliament which on a noteworthy occasion last year he was courageous enough to express. I am looking forward to seeing him exhibit the same courage he did on that quite unusual occasion.
Those who sat in the house last year will well recall the debate on the government measure to continue the Emergency Powers Act for another year, from May 31, 1953, to May 31, 1954. And those same members will not have forgotten that the official opposition, fought up hill and down dale against the continuation of that measure, at every opportunity and every stage. The position we took then was a position of complete, outright and irreconcilable opposition to the continuation of powers of this kind. That was our position at that time, and on August 10 last year, and it is our position today.
Emergency Powers Act
Oh, Oh.
It will not be forgotten-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When there is so much turmoil in the house it should be kept in mind that a point might be brought up on which I would have to rule and, under present circumstances in the house, I would have to admit that I had not heard. I am sure hon. members would want me to hear the hon. member who has the floor. Therefore I would ask them to be silent.

One of the features of the debate which occurred last year was the participation in it of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). He has not yet participated in the present debate. I for one look forward to hearing what he may have to contribute to this debate today.
It will also be remembered that last year some hon. Liberal members of this house did express grave concern over the continuation of these powers. Indeed, one of them had the courage to stand in this house, the then hon. member for London, Mr. Jeffery, and say that he could not support the continuation of this measure were it not for the fact that we were almost certain to have an election in the then succeeding months, and there would be no parliament to be called into session if an emergency did arise.
It will not have been forgotten, either, Mr. Speaker, that the measure to extend this statute passed on second reading only after the Prime Minister had spoken and had given certain very sweeping assurances to the house. Those assurances were to this effect, that the government would not make use of those powers except under the compulsion of grave necessity. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, he said, as you will find recorded at page 3319 of Hansard of March 26, 1953:
I hope it will not have to be used at all.
Well, with these assurances ringing in their ears, the house, on a majority vote, decided to give the government the extension of power for another year which it then so urgently sought. What became of those assurances? The record is quite clear and all too fresh.
Let me first ask the question as to the extent of those powers. The extent of those powers, Mr. Speaker, is such that to most intents and purposes the governor in council may do everything that parliament may do. The words of section 2 of the Emergency Powers Act are sweeping in their breadth. Section 2 reads:
2. (1) The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he
3240	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act
may by reason of the existing international emergency deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
Notice, if you will, the unqualified breadth of these statements, Mr. Speaker. The terms that follow are set forth only for the purpose of clarification. The section proceeds: and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it is hereby declared that the powers of the governor in council shall extend to all matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated, that is to say:
And there follows an enumeration. The only limitation placed by this statute upon these powers, so sweeping and broad in their full amplitude, is to this effect, that those powers do not include the power to make orders or regulations in relation to:
(a)	arrest, except as incidental to proceedings under section three, detention, exclusion or deportation of any person;
(b)	censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings; or
(c)	expenditure of moneys otherwise than in accordance with an appropriation by parliament except expenditure of moneys from any fund or account established by order or regulation in connection with a scheme of control for the purposes of that scheme of control.
There you have, Mr. Speaker, powers that would make any dictator swoon with envy. And, sir, how do they compare with the powers in the statute which the government tells us they do not wish to have occasion to invoke, namely, the War Measures Act? Well, sir, the language of the War Measures Act is virtually identical with that of the section now under discussion with the exception of these excepting words which I have mentioned, and indeed not even all of them. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, with the exception of the power that I have mentioned, it is perfectly clear that under this notorious measure the governor in council possesses power to do everything that the sovereign parliament of Canada itself can do.
This is the year 1954. Why should parliament be any longer a party to abdicating power given to it by the people, given to it by the constitution, in favour of a group of men whom we call the cabinet? Sir, I submit to you that powers as sweeping as those cannot be justified in a democracy in this year of grace 1954.
How does the government justify them? They can only justify them, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of the assertion by parliament of the existence, not in 1944 or 1945, or in the years immediately following the war, but today, 1954, of such an emergency that democracy cannot be permitted to proceed in its normal constitutional and traditional manner.

The statute speaks of an existing international emergency. Well, that is what the statute spoke of in 1951 when it was placed on the statute books. I put this question to hon. members opposite:	What emergency
exists today that is of such a nature that it cannot permit of the continuation of normal constitutional parliamentary processes? What condition exists either in Canada or in the world today that requires that there be on the part of parliament this abdication of powers, that no self-respecting parliament can possibly justify abdicating in favour of a small group of men? What the government has had to say in past time in trying to justify continuation of these sweeping powers under the guise and pretext of emergency was indeed vague. We know the dangers that lurk in the assertion by parliament of the existence of an emergency, sir; for ever since the Nolan case it is clear, if there were any doubt before, that the courts of this land will have no power to examine into the facts to determine whether such a declaration on the part of parliament has authority or justification or not. If parliament will simply say in legislative terms that there exists in Canada today an emergency, then, under that decision, power flows to parliament to legislate even at the expense of the constitutional powers of the provinces.
Sir, we of the official opposition assert that there exists neither in Canada nor in the world today any such condition as justifies this overturn of the processes of democracy.
I next ask the question, sir, what use has been made by the government of those sweeping and arbitrary powers? First, I say, sir, that since this measure was brought into being in 1951, a total of 25 orders in council has been passed under the authority of it: in 1951, 19; in 1952, 5; in 1953, 1.
In the second place, what has been the nature of these orders in council? Well, there has been quite a variety and assortment of them, Mr. Speaker, but this characteristic is common to all of them, that parliament was competent to do everything that every one of these orders in council did.
The third feature is this, Mr. Speaker, that whether parliament was in session or not matters not a whit to this government in exercising these powers. If it happened to suit their convenience to proceed by order in council rather than submit the proposed measure to parliament for enactment here by the elected representatives of the people they went ahead and put it into effect by order in council.
In 1951 the session of parliament began on January 30 and extended to December 29. It is true that parliament was not actually

sitting every day of that period; but if you will simply count the days that parliament did actually sit right here in this room and in the other place you will find, sir, that twelve of those orders in council were passed while parliament was in session.
In 1952, of the five orders in council passed under the authority of this measure three were passed while parliament was actually physically in session here. In 1953 the one order in council that was passed was passed while parliament was in session. Therefore you see, Mr. Speaker, that of the total of 25 orders in council passed under the authority of this notorious measure 16 were passed while parliament was actually sitting here, assembled here for the purpose of doing the business of the country and meeting the legislative needs of Canada.
Let us examine a little more deeply into this question of legislating while parliament is in session. March and April of last year saw events in this house that ought to be carefully observed by every student of constitutional history and by every citizen who is alive to what the rule of law has meant in buttressing the liberties of Canadians and those from whose example we have drawn these liberties. I have mentioned, sir, that the bill was given second reading following assurances given by the Prime Minister to the house on March 26, 1953, very solemn assurances, if I may say so, and it was on April 17 that the government opposite proceeded to tear to shreds and tatters these solemn assurances given to the house by the Prime Minister and accepted by the house in good faith.
What then happened? Without saying a word to parliament the government, on Friday, April 17, went to work and under the authority of the Emergency Powers Act passed order in council No. 1953/604. It was a measure relating to the control of contraband on the China seas. It was not made public on Friday. The house was in session that Friday. It was in session morning, afternoon and evening that day, but not a word was said to the house. On Monday morning, April 20, when here in session the house actually was dealing with amendments to the Canada Shipping Act, of the very same subject matter as the order in council then three days old, still preserved in official secrecy.
The house had certain amendments before it on that Monday morning, April 20, in committee of the whole. It dealt with those amendments and the measure in due course was given third reading and sped on its way to the other place. Fifteen minutes later,
Emergency Powers Act after that measure had safely taken its departure from this house, with a delicate sense of timing the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) came into the house and announced, in the ears of a dumbfounded House of Commons, that this order in council had been passed dealing with the very subject matter that had been before the house only minutes previously.
The official opposition on that occasion, as on this occasion, did its duty and introduced a measure of censure and invited the house to express its censure upon a government that had proven itself so callously, so deliberately forgetful of the promises and solemn assurances given to the house by the Prime Minister less than a month before. You will recall how completely, how tragically the whole attitude of this government towards the House of Commons, towards its constitutional responsibilities, was revealed in the course of that debate by the spokesman for the government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), when he uttered these memorable words recorded for all time in Hansard at page 4197:
If we have overstepped our powers, I make no apology for having done so.
Sir, no Cromwell, no Hitler, no Mussolini, could have put in plainer terms his dictatorial concept of the function and power of government.

speechtext: Order. I have been listening very intently to the remarks of the hon. member, and possibly I should have risen earlier. The hon. member, in language which was very carefully selected, did, in my view, imply that some hon. members have shown bad faith toward the house. He did not mention any one in particular. But later he went on to say, after having referred to one or two cabinet ministers, that they had deliberately forgotten the assurances they had given to the house. The hon. member's language was couched in such learned terms that I did not want to take issue with him and ask him to be careful about the language that he was using, but I am afraid that the leniency I have been showing has perhaps given him some encouragement. He has now reached the point where, I think he will agree with me, the words he has just addressed toward the Minister of Trade and Commerce are not parliamentary. -better calculated to express their conception of power than the words used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on that occasion. I am sure you will give me credit for this, Mr. Speaker. If I had had any idea there was anything unparliamentary about those words I would have refrained from using them. With the greatest respect, I did not undertake to refer to the minister. I referred to his language, and in my humble submission that unfortunate statement by the minister should be open to the strongest form of censure in this house. I am dealing with the words he used and I confined my remarks to the words he used. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I intended nothing unparliamentary. I was not speaking of the minister personally. I confined my remarks to his language.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

I know that sometimes it appears to be difficult for hon. members to withdraw words. When I was a private member I was never called upon to withdraw words, perhaps because I did not take part in debates as often as some hon. members do. To me it is a simple matter to withdraw words which are considered by the Chair to be unparliamentary. Now, the hon. member is reasonable, and I say that in my view it is offensive and unparliamentary to attribute the comments he has to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who is also the Minister of Defence Production. Indeed, had the hon. member used the same words in relation to any other hon. member of this house I would have felt exactly the same way and I would have asked the hon. member to withdraw. I am sure the hon.

member would not have used that expression if this, for example, were just at the end of the war. To say of a cabinet minister that his attitude is comparable with that of Hitler or Mussolini is unparliamentary and I do not believe the hon. member would want to insist upon having these words on the record no matter how strongly he wishes to censure the government at this time. See Beauchesne, third edition, citation 260, which states that no member can be allowed to say that a minister has transferred himself from a constitutional minister into a tyrant.
I do say again to you, sir, with the utmost respect-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am asking the hon. member to withdraw.

I still do not know, Mr. Speaker, what you are asking me to withdraw, but such is my love for you that I will withdraw anything. I am very glad though, Mr. Speaker, that it does not lie within the power of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to withdraw what he said on that occasion. His words are there for all time and they are there for all Canadians who value their rights and privileges to look upon.
If I cannot use the language to which I am accustomed, then I will simply have to resort to Shakespeare:
Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed,
That he is grown so great?
There were two hon. members of the house who on that occasion showed a most commendable degree of courage. The first was the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall). I was hoping he would be in the house at this time. Perhaps he is here. I can hear his voice but I cannot see him. The other member was the then hon. member for London. Be it said to the credit of these two hon. members that for the sake of principle they courageously voted against the government on that occasion and expressed their disapproval of what the government had done.
May I also remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the use of the powers vested in this government has been accompanied by the sort of thing which goes with the exercise of powers such as these in the way in which this government has exercised them. It has bred lawlessness in this government. You will remember very well, Mr. Speaker, that one of the 25 orders in council has been kept secret. Although when parliament passed the statute it called for a tabling of these measures, nevertheless one has still been kept secret from the public by the government.
One last fact worthy of note in relation to the use of the powers under this act is

that since that notorious order in council was passed on April 17, 1953, the government has not found occasion and has not even found the need for any further use of these powers by way of pretext or excuse for the continuation of this measure.
We have had given to us time and time again the threadbare argument that the government must have standby powers in case the international situation should take a turn for the worse. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am going to suggest to you that that argument has been overworked. It is a dead horse now.
In the first place, parliament should be doing the legislating. Parliament can be called to meet upon very short notice. In 1950 parliament met on three days' notice. In the second place, parliament is capable of swift action in an emergency. If we do not believe that, if we do not believe that parliament is capable of appreciating the existence of an emergency and rising to the need in meeting it, then, Mr. Speaker, we have indeed betrayed parliamentary government. Parliament is capable of meeting these situations and we were elected for all such purposes.
In the third place, there evidently will be no election this year. It need not now worry any hon. members that there may not be a parliament in existence for any period during this year.
Then, sir, if an extreme emergency should suddenly and unexpectedly arise, I say to you, sir, that in the first place parliament ought to be summoned. If it is a matter of the gravest emergency, of the kind which faced this country in 1914 or 1939, there are on the statute books statutes capable of dealing with it. There is standby legislation already there.
Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that we of the official opposition have never suggested that the War Measures Act should be invoked in reference to any of these situations to which the government has referred as a pretext for asking parliament to vest in it these emergency powers. We have said no emergency powers are needed to deal with any existing situation.
Let the house remember that there are vast powers conferred on this government by parliament in other measures. Let me remind you, sir, of the very wide powers conferred on this government by the Defence Supplies Act. Under section 3 of that act the Minister of Trade and Commerce may:
(a)	buy or otherwise acquire, exchange, process, develop, repair, maintain, store and transport defence supplies:
Emergency Powers Act
(b)	acquire, store and maintain stocks of strategic materials, and other materials or articles entering into the manufacture of defence supplies or the construction, development, repair or maintenance of projects, and sell or otherwise dispose of such materials or articles and use the whole or any part of the proceeds . . .
And so on. These and more extended provisions in keeping with the sweeping powers conferred upon this government are in the subsection I have just read.
Consider also the provisions of the Defence Production Act, section 15 of which provides that the same minister:
. . . may, on behalf of Her Majesty and subject to the provisions of this act,
(a)	buy or otherwise acquire, utilize, store, transport, sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of defence supplies;
(b)	manufacture or otherwise produce, finish, assemble, process, develop, repair, maintain or service defence supplies or manage and operate facilities therefor;
(c)	construct or acquire defence projects and sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of them;
And so on. That, and another following long list of very wide powers, have been conferred upon the government through the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Let me also remind you, Mr. Speaker, that last week this house approved the extension for a further period of three years of the powers conferred upon this government in relation to the import and export of goods, and giving the governor in council power to impose limitations on the export and import of goods, particularly of strategic materials, except under government licence. Here are sweeping and ample powers adequate to meet the needs of legitimate government necessity under any situation now existing or likely to arise.
We must examine this situation in its essence. Parliament, a free and unfettered parliament, is and historically has been the champion of the rights and the freedoms of the people. Tie the hands of parliament, force on the part of parliament an abdication of its functions and its duties and you have taken the first long step towards intrusion upon and invasion of the rights and privileges of the people.
I have been speaking of the essence of the parliamentary method. The essence of the parliamentary method is just this: Parliament is elected to do all the legislating that is required in the interests of the Canadian people. It is of the essence of the parliamentary method that parliament alone legislates. It is also of the essence of our parliamentary system that the government is responsible to parliament. It is likewise of the essence of the parliamentary system that parliament functions in public, for the public to see and

Emergency Powers Act to judge and tor the public to bring responsible public opinion to bear upon members of parliament.
We are seeing here a renewal of the historic struggle between parliament and the executive branch of government. We see here in this situation and in this parliament, sad to say, a completely inverted relationship. We see a government supreme, tyrannizing over parliament. We see it using its sweeping powers in a way that no government should use them. We also see, Mr. Speaker, existing side by side with parliament another lawmaking body, namely the governor in council. That is a body that does not meet in public but meets in secret, and whose processes are not open to public review and cannot be observed by the public or by parliament before decisions are taken. It is not a proper legislative body, yet it is existing side by side with parliament here as a legislative body. It is functioning in secret and it can function with a quorum of four persons. Mr. Speaker, this is a carryover from the mentality of the war. Surely the time has come for this house to emancipate itself from the mentality of the war. When, if not now, will the government give up these sweeping and arbitrary powers? We have present in this measure all the elements needed to transform the Canadian democracy into a Canadian dictatorship and to transform the Canadian confederation into a centralized form of government. I do not say that this government is going to do that, Mr. Speaker; but our concern in parliament must be not to place it within the power of any government to work that wrong upon our constitution and upon democracy.
Mr. Speaker, under this measure and measures like it there has been under this government a decline of parliament, of respect for parliament and in the position of parliament. In putting forward this amendment we on this side of the house are fighting for the restoration of the power, the prestige, the dignity and the supremacy of parliament. We are fighting for the restoration of democracy. We are fighting for the restoration of parliament to its full vigour and stature as the champion of the rights and freedoms of the people. We are fighting for the restoration of the integrity of the constitution of this country, which has been badly battered at the hands of this government. In a word, Mr. Speaker, we are fighting for the restoration of responsible government. On the vote on this amendment there is now given to every hon. member the opportunity and the challenge to show by his vote where he stands on the issue of responsible government.
(Mr. Fleming.]
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) or the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe).

Mr. Speaker, the remarks made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) prompted me to rise at this time. He is incorrect when he makes the statement that the amendment now before this house gives to hon. members an opportunity of voting on the Emergency Powers Act. That statement is incorrect. Actually there is nothing before this house but a lot of noise.
For a start, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), on the motion to go into supply, moved an amendment to the effect that legislation such as the Emergency Powers Act is offensive to the parliamentary institution. There is not any argument about that fact. There are, however, some things we must remember with regard to the Emergency Powers Act. First, that act is not before the house at the present time and it may automatically cease to exist at the end of May. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made that point quite clear. We are therefore not discussing the Emergency Powers Act at all. There is no proposal to amend it. As to the hon. member who just took his seat, of course it is his job and that of the opposition to beat the government and to prove to the people of Canada that they might do a better job. But I suggest that he is wasting a lot of energy because we are four years away from the time when that would be possible. I think the official opposition are shooting off their ammunition a little bit early, and that their timing is off.
We have lots of ammunition.
It has not been demonstrated in this debate.

That is a matter of opinion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

I like to try to be fair about these things. When the Emergency Powers Act came into existence, the hon. member and all members of this house voted for it.

That is not correct, Mr. Speaker. An examination of the record clearly shows that this measure, on third reading in 1951, passed on division. If the hon. member looks at the record he will find that in what I had to say I was extremely critical.
Were you against it?
Yes. The record clearly shows that it passed on division.

I am not going to quibble about that matter. In 1952 it was passed unanimously. But what brought it into being? The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) made it quite clear that we should not place the government in the position of having to invoke the War Measures Act if certain things had to be done when members were not here. Mind you, I am not saying that I agree with all the things the government does by order in council, but I also want to say this. Regardless of whether the Emergency Powers Act was there on the statute books or not, orders in council would be passed. The revoking of the Emergency Powers Act does not take from the government the right to pass regulations and orders in council. That right would still be there. I call to the attention of hon. members the fact that when section 98 of the Criminal Code was enacted there was no Emergency Powers Act. Nevertheless, a highly offensive statute was placed on the statute books of Canada at that time without an Emergency Powers Act. It took us a long time to get clear of it. I do not need to remind the hon. member what party was in power at that time. All of this argument, to the effect that we are going to abolish orders in council, the right to make regulations and all that kind of stuff by getting rid of the Emergency Powers Act is not correct.
I am afraid that as I see this debate developing, and from what I have read in the press during the past few weeks on other issues, it would seem that most of the arguments I have heard in this debate are a repetition of what I have read in the press
Emergency Powers Act from certain sections of Canada concerning taxing powers. I feel it is well that members should understand that. So far as I am concerned, I am not prepared to stand up in my place and vote on this amendment, thereby leading the people of the country to believe that I am voting to get rid of the Emergency Powers Act; that is not correct. All there is before the house at the moment is an attempt on the part of the opposition to beat the government on this question of too much power.
Now, let us take a fair look at the proposition. All members have stated that while these emergency powers are there, the great objection to them is that they have not been used; that they were not necessary. If they have not been used, then there has not been any undue exercise of power by the government. What brought the Emergency Powers Act into being in the first place was the fact that we were living in a very insecure world. The legislation is offensive because we do not want to be living in that kind of world. When you have to have that kind of legislation it is an indication you are living in that kind of world. In my opinion it is still that kind of world. While you have an uneasy armistice in Korea, no one can say that the war could not flare up again overnight. There was no formal declaration of war when that act of aggression took place. Our allies are fighting in Indo-China, and we are part of that war because we are part of the NATO set-up.
Some members say that it is only a matter of hours to get the members into this house from across Canada. So far as Ontario and Quebec are concerned, that may be true. It certainly is not true of the other parts of Canada. We had the experience of being called here during the railway strike, for example. It was impossible to come here by train, and it was impossible to get here by aeroplane within the time prescribed. I know that I had to drive up here in an automobile. Flying weather is uncertain. It is not correct to say that members can get here within a matter of hours. I suppose the thinking behind that statement is that nothing exists east or west of Ontario and Quebec, because that is the thinking in so far as other things are concerned. It certainly is not correct to say that the members could be here in a matter of hours.
So far as I am concerned, I am not prepared to vote on this propaganda statement; that is exactly what it is. When the Emergency Powers Act is before this house, if it does not expire in May, so far as I am concerned I shall look at the bill in the light of the circumstances then existing in the

Emergency Powers Act world. I am not going to fool anyone now or let anyone fool me into thinking that I am voting on that act this afternoon. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) talked about legislation and the great exercise of powers. I have said a good many times in this house, and I am prepared to say again, that so far as the province from which I come is concerned, if more power were exercised by this government a lot of the chaos that exists in industry and in other fields would not exist. I am not quarrelling with that at all. We have not got the power to legislate upon a lot of the matters upon which we should be legislating. I hope the time will come when we will have that power, because without greater activity on the part of the central government it is impossible to get equality of opportunity in many fields across this country.
I am not prepared at any time to maintain Canada as ten little Canadas rather than one big Canada. There is a lot of legislation that we should be handling in this parliament that would be in the best interests of the Canadian people, but unfortunately there are constitutional bars to that consideration. They will have to be ironed out through the regular democratic processes in consultation with the provinces. I rose to speak because, when the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) was taking his seat, he stated that every member of this house now had the opportunity of showing where he stood on the Emergency Powers Act. I wanted to make it quite clear that he was not fooling me. So far as I am concerned, he is not going to fool the country into believing this vote has anything to do with the Emergency Powers Act. I will oppose the government on a lot of things they are doing, and they would be doing those things if the Emergency Powers Act were not there, such as making agreements, arrangements, and issuing statements to the press that should be issued in this house. However, that has nothing to do with this debate. So far as I am concerned, I am going to vote against this motion, and reserve my vote for the time when the matter is in issue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like, if I had no other reason for rising to my feet, to offer congratulations to the two last speakers. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) by asking two questions shed more light upon this whole matter than had been shed by several preceding speeches from the opposite side of the chamber. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) continued the work of clarification that was begun by the two questions asked by the hon. member for Fort


William. I wonder whether the hon. member for Cape Breton South will permit me to continue the process a little bit farther?
There is not only as he has suggested the matter of creating great sound and fury in this chamber in connection with this general subject matter. There is something even more serious than that involved, in my opinion, and that becomes quite clear when one carefully reads the resolution moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). It reads:
this house desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
Who granted those powers to the governor in council, Mr. Speaker? This parliament did so by the Emergency Powers Act. What the hon. member is urging, instead of bringing in a bill to repeal the Emergency Powers Act, is that parliament should criticize parliament for having given those powers to the governor general in council. Now, I know -that it has been customary for our hon. friends in the opposition to attribute to the government, as if it were the fault of the government, the actions of this parliament, upon the ground that members of parliament who were elected to support the government should not carry out the mandate they have received from the people, upon the rather strange ground that they should not support government legislation when they come to parliament. But I would suggest, sir, that in casting their votes in this parliament in a manner to carry out the mandate they have received from their electors, they are not acting in any capacity other than as members of parliament, and the law which they vote for and the law which is passed, in this case the Emergency Powers Act, giving these powers to the governor general in council, is a law for which none other than parliament is responsible. Therefore, it seems to me that, sir, without raising any point of order-because I understand Your Honour has said Your Honour is prepared to receive this resolution which we are now discussing-it is very regrettable indeed that a statute which has been passed by this parliament-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: By the last parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, by the last parliament, but by the parliament of Canada at the time- should be stated as a grievance which the opposition tries to raise against the government on a motion to go into supply. Because, Mr. Speaker, if it is possible to do that in connection with this particular statute, why is it not possible in respect of any other statute on the statute books of the country? In that way, sir, a small minority group in

this parliament could postpone indefinitely parliament getting into committee of supply to consider the estimates-which, in my judgment, is one of the most important functions parliament has to perform, and one which is not always too well or too faithfully discharged because of the tendency upon the part of certain members in the house to protract debates upon other matters, so that there is not time left properly to consider the estimates.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has pointed out, at least by implication, surely if there were a sincere desire here to permit the house at this time to vote upon the question of the Emergency Powers Act, the proper method to have followed would have been for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) to bring in a bill to repeal the Emergency Powers Act.
It is quite true that if he did not bring in that bill, the present act would expire by the mere efflux of time on May 31 next-and without all this debate and sound and fury. And it is also true that if, under the world circumstances existing in, we will say, the middle of May next, the government considered that it was warranted in asking parliament to give another year's extension of the powers in the Emergency Powers Act, a debate would then ensue upon that piece of legislation, in connection with which all the oratory we have heard today, in the abstract, could be much more pertinently, more relevantly and therefore more cogently applied to the question as to whether these emergency powers should or should not be extended for another year.
But if my hon. friends of the official opposition, not being content to wait for a few weeks until they could see what precisely were the circumstances in which the question as to whether the Emergency Powers Act should be extended would be decided, desire at this present time to have the house vote upon the principle of the legislation, then surely the sensible course for them to have followed would have been to bring a bill into the house to repeal the present Emergency Powers Act forthwith.
Nothing could be more ridiculous than that they should ask parliament to censure parliament in respect of that for which only parliament is responsible, namely the passage of the Emergency Powers Act, giving certain powers to the governor general in council. Supposing this amendment were to carry: would not the Canadian parliament cut a fine figure among intelligent people throughout the world when it became known that, in 1954, it had solemnly got together
Emergency Powers Act and, after careful consideration, upon motion of the Leader of the Opposition, had solemnly resolved that parliament-
-desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
Or, in other words, my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition is asking that this parliament in 1954 move a vote of want of confidence in itself for what it did in 1953; only that and nothing more.
And it is not as if he needed to employ this particular vehicle to register the dissent of his party in this matter. For, by merely the efflux of time, perhaps the whole matter would have cleared itself without any debate at all. But if he could not wait until that time came, and wished to bring the matter before parliament in a form in which we could vote upon it with some dignity, then he should have brought in his bill forthwith to repeal the Emergency Powers Act.
For that reason, and for that reason primarily, and without going into all the arguments which the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) repeated this afternoon, I should think for perhaps the third or fourth time in the house, for my part I am quite content to vote against the amendment upon the ground that it is purely vexatious, and that it would be highly embarrassing to parliament itself for us to pass it.

Mr. Speaker, the smokescreen of
complicated verbiage which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has just tried to throw all around this question has been extremely well done. I congratulate him as a producer of smokescreens. I am glad the minister has asked that question, because I am coming to it. In the course of his remarks he made the statement that it would not be right for parliament to censure parliament, and referred to the possibility of parliament in 1954 censuring parliament in 1953.
Mr. Speaker, the system of Canadian government is such that parliament is composed

Emergency Powers Act of certain parties. The gentlemen who now form the government belong to a certain party. Any action this amendment suggests is not censuring parliament as such; I would feel that it is more definitely censuring actions this government has taken in past years, and particularly in 1953, when, over the vocal opposition of this party, it insisted upon perpetuating this iniquitous legislation.
I was most interested yesterday and again today to hear certain references to past statements by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) and-I do not know which title to use, whether it should be the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) or the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I was just thinking how these clarified certain issues, and that at this point those gentlemen might be all right if only they could shut their mouths retroactively. Since they cannot do that, we have now set on the record for all time to come an attitude which is not good for the perpetuation of a free democratic government in this country.
It seems to me that it is wrong in this enlightened mid-twentieth century that this government, not this House of Commons but this government, should wish to deprive this house as a whole of powers which men have fought and died for almost since the dawn of history.
Three names were linked earlier today in a certain connection. Two of them were fairly recent, the third was not. The third was that of Cromwell of many hundreds of years ago. In the fight, turmoil and heat of that time we forged traditions and principles which have come down to us almost intact until the present time. During the past war the government instituted certain measures which may have been necessary at that time, but which they have perpetuated unto the present in a most unnecessary fashion.
It is almost axiomatic that once powers have been conceded to an executive committee for a special emergency-and originally that was the basis of this legislation- there is a deep-rooted resistance by that executive to the suggestion that they should be surrendered, even though the emergency is long past. It seems to me that was made crystal clear by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself yesterday in only one sentence, Mr. Speaker, when he said in the course of his remarks, as reported at page 3217 of Hansard:
I do not foresee any immediate occasion or any immediate reason for having to exercise the powers under the act.
If there is no immediate occasion and if there is no immediate reason, why then


does he remain silent in the face of the repeated suggestions that these powers should be repealed? He does not want them; the government say they do not want to use them; and yet they want to keep them for some indefinite, unknown, vague reason in the future. It is the most specious argument, Mr. Speaker, that it is possible to introduce in support of this legislation which we dislike so vehemently.
A book was published recently called "The Passing of Parliament". Were I in a position to do so I should like to make it required reading at least for the gentlemen of the treasury benches, because it might gnaw at their vitals a little bit. As was pointed out very clearly, some of the things they are doing are not perhaps in the best democratic tradition, and there is one quotation from this book that I should like to introduce at this point. It is found at page 7, and reads as follows:
In the last half-century there has been a shift in the centre of gravity from the floor of the House of Commons to the offices of the great departments of state, where in reality policy is framed. Parliament becomes year by year less of a governing council and more of a censor of executive acts.
It is hardly in the tradition of this house, and particularly it is hardly in the tradition of this great party, that we should sit here quietly and acquiesce in that shift and in that gradual closing down and further and further delimitation of the powers, responsibilities and opportunities of this house to examine the legislation which comes before us. Because this issue is so clear, because it is so definite, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that I need to take up any more time of the house save for a moment to look once again at the wording of this amendment. It is one of the interesting aspects of this debate that the amendment has been repeated so many times. Perhaps the reason for that is that the amendment carries within itself the great weight of debate that should force people to vote in its favour, because it says:
this house desires to record its opinion that the powers granted to the governor in council under the Emergency Powers Act are repugnant to responsible parliamentary government.
The powers which are granted under that legislation are powers which should normally be exercised by this house. To the extent that they have been taken away from this house we have lost something which has been traditionally and rightly ours. To the extent that the gentlemen on the treasury benches and the others behind them, who speak so little, oppose this amendment, they are defending the type of government, or the tendency toward the type of government,

which is one that we have fought against and as a nation we have opposed throughout our history.
I have one more thing to say. I am delighted to see the gentlemen over there and the gentlemen to my left working together and agreeing in their attitude on this legislation, because, Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing which the gentlemen to my left will need if-and I hope it never comes-they come into power in this country, it is some measure by which they can cloak the actions which they will want to take to turn us into a socialist state, some measure by which, without proper supervision by this house, they can proceed to do things which the people of this country would not want to approve. And I suggest that when we see these two groups linked in opposing this amendment we begin to see come out from underneath the dark clouds and from underneath the covers some of the very objectionable features of this government.

Canada Grain Act

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of the house a grievance having to do with a motion adopted by the committee on agriculture during the last session of parliament recommending that the government should consider the advisability of referring the Canada Grain Act to this committee on agriculture for study at a future session of parliament. Also, the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in reply to a question I asked him on this matter on December 16. My question, as reported at page 970 of Hansard, was as follows:
Can the minister say whether the committee on agriculture and1 colonization will he called together early in the new year in order to review the Canada Grain Act, as recommended by that committee at the last session of the house? As the minister is aware, it would be called for the purpose of discussing the question of overages and box car distribution.
To this the minister replied:
My hon. friend is aware that it is not the duty of any minister to call committees together. As a member of the committee in question, my hon. friend is in a position to do so. I have no amendments to the Canada Grain Act to recommend. There will be later in the session matters that I will wish to refer to the committee; but the subject matter of its business, I assume, will be determined by the committee.
I asked this supplementary question:
Has the minister any objection to the government's carrying out the committee's recommendation, that the Canada Grain Act be referred to the committee on agriculture for study?
To this the minister replied:
I have nothing to do with the matter. If the committee meets and desires to undertake that work, I shall endeavour to co-operate. But I have no wish either that it should be done or should not be done.
Following that statement by the minister, Mr. Speaker, I communicated with the chairman of the agriculture committee, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), and I suggested to him that the committee should be called together to consider whether at this session we should undertake a review of the Canada Grain Act.
In reply to my letter the hon. member for Provencher pointed out, I believe quite correctly, that according to the standing orders of this house a committee can only consider matters which have been referred to it by the house. Therefore, according to the chairman of the committee, the committee can undertake a review of the Canada Grain Act only when a motion is passed by the house directing that such a review be undertaken.
On Monday, March 15, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) presented a motion to refer the annual report of the
[Mr. Speaker.)
Canadian wheat board, together with the annual report of the board of grain commissioners, to the committee on agriculture. My point is that in that recommendation there was no inclusion of a study of the Canada Grain Act as recommended by the committee on agriculture during the last session of parliament. On the important issue of reviewing the Canada Grain Act, which has not had a general overhaul since 1930, the minister says it is up to members of the committee. Then when a member of the committee endeavours to have the committee undertake such a review he finds that, according to the chairman, a committee can undertake the review only when matters are referred to it by the house and when those matters are included in its terms of reference.
I think that the members of the committee on agriculture last session unanimously came to the conclusion that it was time for an overhaul of the Canada Grain Act. Certainly they came to the conclusion that it was time a thorough study was made of the provisions of the Canada Grain Act.
The Canada Grain Act came into existence in 1912, being a substitute then for a previous act, namely the Manitoba grain act. There was a general overhaul in 1930. There has been no substantial review of the Canada Grain Act since 1930. By refusing to refer the Canada Grain Act to the committee on agriculture I think the government is breaking faith with and flouting the wishes of the members of that previous committee. That previous committee of this house studied the Canada Grain Act and found that a further review should' take place. Last year we held quite a number of meetings. Our evidence extended to 162 pages and we discovered, with respect to the Canada Grain Act and its administration, a great many things that should be the subject of review. The whole question of grain overages was a bone of contention. I think it is fair to say that the members of the board of grain commissioners left a great many questions unanswered. There were put to the members of the board some extremely important questions that they were unable to answer.
I think our experience last year demonstrates that there needs to be an overhaul in the personnel of the board of grain commissioners. Certainly there needs to be a review of the authority contained in the Canada Grain Act. We were unable to get information as to the quantity of grain that was lost through drying. We were unable to get a breakdown of hundreds of thousands of bushels of overages and shortages in the various grades other than the straight commercial grades. We reviewed what has since

come to be known as the Brancepeth case where a farmer endeavoured to demand the right to unload his grain at the elevator. To say the least, the evidence we received in that committee was highly conflicting. The authorities in charge, according to the evidence they submitted to that committee, were anything but consistent in the stand they had taken in relation to this particular case. I think it is time that that part of the Canada Grain Act was reviewed so that we may find out once and for all just what a farmer's rights are under the present act; and in the light of that information the committee can consider whether or not changes should be made in the present Canada Grain Act.
There is one further thing that came before the committee last year that should be thoroughly reviewed, in my opinion, during the present session, namely the section of the act dealing with the distribution of box cars. The distribution of box cars is a bone of contention in western Canada. I have certain ideas as to how box cars can better be distributed. The minister has said that those particular ideas would not work out satisfactorily. However, of this I am sure. If the committee on agriculture is requested to review the section of the Canada Grain Act having to do with the distribution of box cars and the car order book, and if we are given the right to call witnesses from the various farm organizations, a workable solution to this problem can be obtained.
My point in rising this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, is simply this. As reported at page 970 of Hansard, of December 16, 1953, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) informed me how the committee itself might undertake a review of the Canada Grain Act. He went further. He told us he had no opinion himself as to whether the Canada Grain Act should or should not be reviewed at the present session. I now inform him that I have endeavoured to have the committee called together as he suggested in the statement to which I have referred and that as a member of the committee I am informed by the chairman that I have not the right to have the committee consider such a review. In the light of the experience we had last year in the committee, the evidence given in that committee, and the fact that a recommendation was made to this house asking that the Canada Grain Act be referred to the committee at a future session of parliament, I ask the minister now whether he will not during this session present a motion referring the Canada Grain Act to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization for review.
Canada Grain Act
I want to say that, as to any questions I have placed on the order paper this session with regard to some of the matters I have raised, the answers have been much better than those I have received previously; the answers have been much more complete. However, I suggest to the minister that referring the report of the board of grain commissioners covering a period of time that is already in the past is not sufficient and that the members of the committee on agriculture should be given the right and the authority to review the act and to see whether the points in the act that apparently do not completely meet with the wishes of the western producers at this time cannot be met by suggested amendments. I can certainly see no harm in the committee's undertaking such a review. I think a great deal of benefit might result from it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the minister in charge of the Canada Grain Act has followed the usual practice. As soon as the report of the board of grain commissioners was available it was tabled and referred to the committee. I have attended the committee in the last few years and I have never known of any reluctance on the part of the committee, in studying the report of the board, to discuss the Canada Grain Act. It always has been discussed and, I presume, not without authority. Certainly the discussion has usually hinged on the terms of the Canada Grain Act. The report of the wheat board was also tabled as soon as it was available, and with the report of the board of grain commissioners is referred to the committee. The committee is now free to proceed to study both reports, and I presume it has ample latitude to study the foundation of the report, which is the legislation that brings both of those organizations into being.
My hon. friend said, why not have the committee start at the beginning of the session and make a complete review? I do not recall any government saying to any committee of this house, take this act and tell us what is wrong with it. If the government knows of anything wrong with an act the government puts forward an amendment of its own, sends that to a committee and allows the committee to deal with the amendment and with the act as it sees fit. However, I have asked the board of grain commissioners if they know of any desirable amendment, and I am told that they have nothing to suggest. I have discussed the matter with farm organizations, and I find that they have nothing concrete to suggest.

Canada Grain Act
The hon. member has referred to the matter of the distribution of box cars. My hon. friend has closed that door himself. He has advocated his ideas on the floor of the house, and his bill has been rejected by the house. Surely he does not expect to have another debate on the distribution of box cars at this session. I believe that is quite obvious. I have never tried to minimize the discussion of wheat matters. I have gone beyond the ordinary rule in answering questions in this house. I have answered questions that under the practice built up over the years perhaps should not have been answered. Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to call the attention of the government to a matter which is highly important for the citizens of this country.
The legislature of the province of Quebec has recently passed an act levying a personal income tax. The main object of this bill is to safeguard the autonomy of the province in the educational field, and to assist universities by giving them grants. It also provides for social and health improvements. In other words, the purpose of this bill is to promote the interests and the welfare of the people.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, excellent in its principle and purpose, this act has the approval of all who consider the prime interest of their country above party politics. The federal authorities are now constitutionally bound to co-operate in its operation.
Among the exclusive powers of provincial legislatures under section 92 of the British North America Act, we find "Direct Taxation within the Province". It is true, however, that section 91 recognizes the right of the federal parliament to "raise money by any mode or system of taxation". These wordings are not contradictory; rather they indicate that the provinces, with an exclusive right on direct taxation, have unquestionable priority in that field.
Until the end of the first world war, that is for nearly half a century, the central government generally refrained from resorting to this taxation. It was only in 1917, after


solemn statements to the effect that this encroachment was only temporary, that it entered this field, never to leave again.
In 1942, the provinces made an agreement with the federal government, under which they yielded, for the duration of the war, their right to levy personal income tax, as well as the tax on corporation income and capital. The federal government then formally undertook to facilitate the use of these sources of revenue by the provinces at the end of the war. The agreement prescribed that:
The federal government shall have the exclusive right to collect personal and corporation income tax for the calendar year ending on the thirty-first day of December nearest to the date of termination of the present agreement and undertakes to reduce the rates of the said personal and corporation income taxes, for the next calendar year, by an amount sufficient to allow the province to re-enter the field of personal and corporation income tax and particularly to reduce its rate of taxation on corporation revenues by at least 10 per cent of such revenues.
In 1941 the Hon. Mr. Ilsley stated: "It is proposed, therefore, as a temporary expedient for the duration of the war only, to ask the provinces to vacate these two tax fields". The minister of finance was referring to personal and corporation income taxes, recognizing at the same time that these taxes rightly belonged to the provinces.
According to official statistics the net income of the ten provinces of the Canadian confederation for the fiscal year 1952-1953 amounted to $1,220,889,000; the government's contribution to this over-all budget was $333,277,000, which represented 27-3 per cent of the grand total. From that federal source, the province of Quebec received $4,211,000, that is 1-49 per cent of its total budget for the fiscal year, of $281,735,000. The details are as follows:

In 1952-1953, a federal contribution of $20,107,000, or 62-05 per cent of the total revenues of $30,925,000 of Newfoundland, was received by that province. As may be seen, Quebec's refusal, in principle, to enter into tax-rental agreements which are profitable to other provinces, can be quite costly.
An editorial published in Le Soleil, a Liberal party organ, reads in part as follows:
So much the better for them, until the day when they may perhaps regret having thus forsaken part of their jurisdiction for the benefit of a centralizing government.
It continues:
It remains doubtful whether the governments of those provinces have the right to commit in such a way, for so long if not forever, assets and powers granted to them by the British North America Act. However, it is up to the legal experts to study this important point. In the meantime, without recrimination and without envy, French Canada regrets it has not their strong support in its demands for privileges, rights and powers it has particular reason to defend as a sacred heritage.
Indeed, the province of Quebec is sustaining heavy material losses in having to fight alone against the encroachments of a centralizing government. Whatever financial hardships it may endure, it considers as even more important privileges and freedoms recognized by various treaties in which British honour was involved. Those privileges and freedoms have been guaranteed by the confederative pact and without that guarantee, our religious and political leaders would have been wary to approve it. In addition to what she may derive from her inheritance, the province of Quebec is determined to keep control over her civil laws, her education and religious freedoms and her social traditions. She is counting on the fairness of her witnesses and friends in the other provinces to recognize eventually that her cause is just and honourable.
Mr. Leopold Richer, in Notre Temps of February 13 last, expressed the opinion that-
-a province that lives on federal grants (statutory or not) is no longer free-
The arrangements between the federal government and the other provinces are merely temporary expedients which the federal government wants to place on a permanent basis and which only tend to aggravate the present constitutional difficulties without bringing about a satisfactory solution. It is a discriminatory system. On the other hand, it is incorrect to allege that these arrangements entail a lessening of the taxation burden. The state does not create wealth; its function is merely to redistribute the revenue collected from the taxpayers.
